paper_title: Write, Evolve, Read: Streaming Cameras into a Persistent World State for 4D Occupancy Forecasting

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: 4D occupancy forecasting predicts the 3D semantic occupancy of a driving scene seconds ahead. Over a few seconds, the scene changes little while the vehicle moves, so most of the space ahead has already been seen. Sorting the future into unchanged, changed, and unseen space, we find that current camera-based world models fall short on the unchanged part: they fail to hold on to what they have already seen, rather than to forecast what will change. We therefore make what the model has seen its state. PersistWorld streams camera frames into a persistent 3D world state anchored in the scene, writing each frame once instead of rebuilding the state from past frames. The state is learned end to end with the forecast, and an evolver predicts it at any queried time along the ego trajectory. On Occ3D-nuScenes, PersistWorld raises the IoU of the best camera-based world model by 19 points at 1-3 s and by 18 to 24 points up to 8 s, while running more than twice as fast. Code and models: https://github.com/wangzian828/PersistWorld. Project page: https://wangzian828.github.io/PersistWorld

sections.content: 4D occupancy forecasting predicts the 3D semantic occupancy of driving scene seconds ahead. Over few seconds, the scene changes little while the vehicle moves, so most of the space ahead has already been seen. Sorting the future into unchanged, changed, and unseen space, we find that current camera-based world models fall short on the unchanged part: they fail to hold on to what they have already seen, rather than to forecast what will change. We therefore make what the model has seen its state. PersistWorld streams camera frames into persistent 3D world state anchored in the scene, writing each frame once instead of rebuilding the state from past frames. The state is learned end to end with the forecast, and an evolver predicts it at any queried time along the ego trajectory. On Occ3D-nuScenes, PersistWorld raises the IoU of the best camera-based world model by 19 points at 13 and by 18 to 24 points up to 8 s, while running more than twice as fast. Code: https://github.com/wangzian828/PersistWorld Project: https://wangzian828.github.io/PersistWorld Figure 2. Two questions sort every occupied voxel of the future scene into unchanged, changed, or unseen space. Beside each kind: its share of the occupied future on Occ3D-nuScenes at 1 and 8 s. 1. Introduction An autonomous vehicle must anticipate how the space around it will be occupied few seconds ahead. Occupancy world models forecast future 3D semantic occupancy from past observations and the planned ego trajectory, and much of the work on them has gone into the forecasting itself: how to tokenize the scene, how to generate its future, and how to condition it on the ego trajectory [9, 11, 26, 35, 47]. Yet with cameras, the setting that matters in practice, they remain far less accurate than models given ground-truth occupancy [6, 9, 26]. Where do their errors lie? Over few seconds, driving scene itself changes little, while the vehicle moves through it. Most of the space ahead of the vehicle has therefore already been seen by its cameras. We make this precise by sorting the future scene into three kinds of space (Figs. 1 and 2): unchanged space, seen and still the same; changed space, seen but different by then; and unseen space, never seen. One second ahead, four fifths of the occupied future is unchanged space; changed space stays small, and unseen space grows only as the vehicle moves into regions it could not see. Current camera-based world models lose much of exactly this part. SparseWorld-TC [9], the strongest of them, reaches an IoU of only 51.07 on unchanged space  (Fig. 1)  , where the scene as seen is already the answer. Its own estimate of the current frame, moved to the target time without any forecasting, already reaches 48.68 there, and the occupancy that STCOcc [25] predicts for two-stage methods reaches 46.31 (Sec. 4.3). Where forecasting is actually needed, on changed and unseen space, SparseWorld-TC is far ahead of carrying the seen scene forward, with an IoU of 45.35 and 40.92 against 26.33 and 0. The shortfall of camera-based world models thus lies not in forecasting what will change but in holding on to what they have already seen, which models given ground-truth occupancy receive for free. The same property of driving scenes also tells how to hold on to it: over few seconds, the cameras view the same, largely unchanged scene from many positions. We therefore make what the model has seen its state: 3D world state anchored in the scene, written directly from camera images and learned end to end with the forecast. The state stays in place as the vehicle moves, so the evidence that every frame provides about place accumulates at one position. To forecast, an evolver predicts the features of the state at the queried time along the ego trajectory. Holding what has been seen in state also makes forecasting cheap. Since consecutive frames show nearly the same scene, the state is updated frame by frame as the images stream in: each new frame only adds its own evidence, as in streaming models that estimate the present scene [5, 32, 49] or keep memory for forecasting [29]. Each image is thus processed once, and no separate perception network is needed, whereas sparse end-to-end models re-derive the scene from the image history for every forecast [7, 9] and two-stage methods first run perception network [6, 11, 26, 35]. Since forecast needs only recent view of the surroundings, the state is reset periodically and keeps only the last few seconds of observation. On Occ3D-nuScenes, our model raises the IoU and mIoU of the best camera-based world model by 19.13 and 3.32 at 13 and runs more than twice as fast. Its IoU rises from 51.07 to 70.86 on unchanged space and from 40.92 to 62.71 on unseen space, and the same model leads by 18.19 to 24.41 IoU at every horizon up to 8 s. Our contributions are: An analysis that sorts the future scene into unchanged, changed, and unseen space, and shows that camera-based world models fall short in holding on to what they have already seen rather than in forecasting what will change. camera-based occupancy world model that holds what it has seen in 3D world state anchored in the scene, written from images, learned end to end with the forecast, updated as stream, and reset periodically. State-of-the-art camera-based forecasting on Occ3DnuScenes at 13 and 18 with single model, which is also the fastest of the compared methods. 2. Related Work Occupancy from cameras. Camera-based occupancy perception lifts image features into 3D grid of semantic voxels, through view transformation into birds-eye-view or voxel features [21, 22], sparse queries [27, 38], or 3D Gaussians [14], and is evaluated on benchmarks such as Occ3D [37] and PanoBench [10]. Rendering-based methods add supervision along camera rays, rendering depth and semantics from the predicted volume [13, 33] or rendering both the prediction and the voxel labels and comparing them in the views or along the rays [3, 18]. We use the same kind of signal, predicting occupancy along each camera ray and supervising it with labels rendered from the ground-truth grid, so that the evidence of each image is written at the right depth along its rays. Temporal methods carry information across frames by propagating object queries [39] or fusing long history through temporal stereo [34]; for occupancy, they evolve 3D Gaussians with ego and object motion [49], stream voxel features [32], or unify several temporal cues [5], and such memory state can also be learned from multi-camera video as pre-training for perception and planning [30]. All these methods estimate the present scene, and every new frame corrects their state. Our state is also updated as stream, but it is learned with the forecast and advanced to future times, where no new frame corrects it. Forecasting the future scene. Occupancy world models tokenize the scene and generate its future autoregressively or by diffusion [11, 15, 16, 26, 4043, 46, 47], warp the current scene to the future ego poses [6], add conditions [12, 19, 45], or separate ego motion from scene change [35]. They are commonly evaluated on Occ3D-nuScenes at 1, 2, and 3 [47], and up to 8 in later work [9, 35]. These models take occupancy as input; with cameras, they forecast from separately trained perception network [22, 25], so what they 2 Figure 3. Overview of PersistWorld. Top: the world state is updated once per capture group; the Evolver, marked E, carries it to the capture time of the next group, and the Writer, marked W, writes the new images into it; is reset to the initial state every eight capture groups. To forecast, the Evolver predicts the state at queried time tk from and the ego trajectory, and the Reader, marked R, decodes it in the queried ego frame. Bottom: the internal operations of each component, Secs. 3.23.4. The grid loss supervises the current and future occupancy, and the ray loss supervises the ray-depth sections of the Writer. Images and ground-truth occupancy, seen from above, are from nuScenes validation scene. forecast from is fixed before forecasting, and such chains degrade when errors enter upstream [48]. Camera-based endto-end models learn the forecast from images [20, 24, 28, 31, 44]; some re-read the image history with sparse queries for every forecast [79], and some can be queried at any time [1, 4]. persistent scene state has also been kept, but from birds-eye-view features [29]. PersistWorld holds what it has seen in 3D world state written directly from images and updated as stream, instead of re-deriving the scene for each forecast. Which parts of the future must be forecast has also been studied: aggregating past observations is strong baseline [17], most occupied future voxels are static [35], and scene evolution has been split into static, moving, and newly observed parts [2, 28, 49]. We split the future by what the input frames have seen into unchanged, changed, and unseen space, and use the split to measure how each kind changes with the horizon and show that camera-based world models fall short on space they have already seen. 3. Method Overview. PersistWorld holds what its cameras have seen in world state on fixed 3D lattice and updates it as stream, once per capture group. capture group, which we also call frame, is the surround-view images taken at one time, together with their camera parameters and the ego pose  (Fig. 3)  . When group arrives, the State Evolver carries to its capture time (Sec. 3.3), the Visibility-aware State Writer writes the evidence of the new images into it (Sec. 3.2), and the Pose-queried Occupancy Reader decodes the current occupancy (Sec. 3.4). To forecast, the Evolver predicts the state at each queried time from and the ego trajectory, and the Reader decodes occupancy in the queried ego frame. All components are trained end to end together with the image backbone (Secs. 3.5 and 3.6). 3.1. World State The state lives on lattice of 1.6 cells anchored in the scene, so cell keeps its address while the vehicle moves. The region queried at any time is the occupancy volume around the ego, 80 80 6.4 on Occ3D, and spans 50 50 4 cells. Each cell stores feature that packs the features of its 2 2 2 sub-cells of 0.8 m, together with the time of its estimate and the time of its last observation, which condition the Evolver (Sec. 3.3). Packing keeps attention in the Evolver over compact lattice, while the Writer and Reader operate on the finer sub-cells; the Reader decodes each sub-cell into 2 2 2 voxels of 0.4 (Sec. 3.4). The state is stored only where it has been written; an unwritten cell takes learned initial feature of its ego-relative position. 3 3.2. Visibility-aware State Writer Images are encoded by DINOv3 ViT-B/16 [36] whose last blocks are fine-tuned, and key and value maps are projected from its feature map. Each capture group is encoded and written once, into the state that the Evolver has just carried to its capture time. For sub-cell with center x, the Writer samples keys and values bilinearly at the projection of into each camera, shifted by small image-plane offset predicted from the sub-cells feature, and adds learned camera embedding. Because the state is already at the capture time, the Writer only places what the new images show and needs no motion model; all motion is left to the Evolver. Ray-depth sections. All sub-cells along pixel ray project to the same image location and sample the same feature, so projection alone cannot tell them apart. We split each patch ray into depth sections of 0.8 and let light head predict, for every patch, distribution over the section that holds the first occupied surface, with one more bin for rays that hit no surface. For each sample, the section containing the sub-cell provides geometry embedding that is added to the key and value, and the log-probability of that section is added as an attention bias, so evidence is weighted by how plausible it is that the sub-cell is the visible surface. Update. The sub-cell feature attends, with single query, to its samples from all cameras and to null token with zero key and value, which lets it take no evidence when no camera shows it. gate from the prior and the candidate feature controls the residual update and is zero where no camera sees, so those keep the state carried by the Evolver. 3.3. State Evolver The Evolver advances the state from the time of its estimate to target time under the ego trajectory. It carries the state to the capture time before writing and predicts the state Its inputs are the state in at each queried future time. window around the ego at the target time and the sequence of ego poses since the last reset (Sec. 3.6) up to the target pose. Motion tokens are formed from the relative SE(3) transforms between consecutive poses and the time steps; each cell attends only to the motion that follows its own estimate, and is conditioned on the age of its estimate and of its last observation. context of the observed state, encoded by further axial blocks over all stored cells, is computed once per update of the state, shared by every advance from it, and added to the cell features before the residual blocks. Residual blocks, with adaptive layer normalization conditioned on these ages, each apply cross-attention to the motion tokens and self-attention along one lattice axis. The output is change added to the state, scaled by the elapsed time, so that the Evolver is the identity when no time passes. Since the ego trajectory up to the target is an input, the same Evolver serves every horizon. 3.4. Pose-queried Occupancy Reader The Reader unpacks the sub-cells and applies local residual block of depth-wise 33 convolution and point-wise mixing, followed by linear layer that predicts class logits for the 2 2 2 voxels of 0.4 inside each sub-cell; the logits are resampled into the queried ego frame. The same Reader decodes the current occupancy right after writing and the future occupancy from the predicted states. 3.5. Gradients are truncated to the last two writes before each loss: the earlier writes run without gradient, so memory does not grow with the segment length. Each image is encoded once per segment. 4. Experiments 4.1. Setup the intersection over union of occupied voxels, IoU, and its mean over the semantic classes, mIoU, inside the camera mask of the target frame. For long-horizon forecasting, we query the same model at every horizon from 1 to 8 s. Streaming evaluation. Our model processes each validation scene as stream of keyframes, as it would run on vehicle. Each capture group is written into the state once, and each keyframe is answered with the state at that moment, which holds one to eight capture groups (Sec. 3.6). As in training, the state is reset at the start of each scene and after every eight capture groups. Dataset and metrics. Occ3D-nuScenes [37] provides 700 training and 150 validation scenes with 18-class labels at 0.4 m. Following SparseWorld-TC [9], forecast uses at most the last eight capture groups and the ground-truth future ego poses. We forecast 1, 2, and 3 ahead from every validation keyframe, which gives 6019 anchor keyframes with 5719, 5419, and 5119 targets at 1, 2, and 3 s. We report Implementation details. Three Kinds of Space Where forecasts fall short. We split the occupied future by the two questions of Sec. 1, using the ground truth of the input frames. Unchanged space makes up 80.85% of it at 1 and 34.87% at 8 s, unseen space grows from 14.39% to 62.06%, and changed space stays below 5%  (Fig. 2)  . Fig. 5a scores the forecasts at 13 on each kind. Our model leads SparseWorld-TC, the strongest prior camera-based world model, at every horizon, and the lead grows with the horizon, from 18.19 to 20.14 IoU and from 3.04 to 3.63 mIoU. SparseWorld-TC does far better than this copy on changed and unseen space but reaches only 51.07 IoU on unchanged space, where the seen scene is already the answer. Our model reaches 70.86 there and 62.71 on unseen space, 19.79 and 21.79 above it. What is seen and what is forecast. To see what forecasting adds, we copy each models estimate of the current frame forward in the same way; for our model, this is Perception + warp in Fig. 5a. On unchanged space, the copy already reaches 68.60 IoU for our model and 48.68 for SparseWorldTC, close to their forecasts of 70.86 and 51.07, and the occupancy that STCOcc [25] predicts for two-stage methods reaches 46.31. Forecasting adds about as much there to both models, 2.26 and 2.39 IoU. Accuracy on unchanged space is thus decided before forecasting, and our lead there comes from how well the model holds on to what it has seen. On changed and unseen space, our forecast exceeds the copy by 4.46 and 37.48 IoU; this is what forecasting adds. Visibility. The state also keeps what has left the view of the cameras. Fig. 5b splits the future by visibility at the last input frame. On space seen only in earlier frames, our model reaches 70.41 IoU, slightly above the 68.99 on space still in view, so what has left the view is not lost. 4.4. Ablation Study Properties of the state. Tab. 3 changes one property of the state at time and scores each variant on the three kinds of space. The state must be anchored in the scene: with an ego-centric state, whose lattice moves with the vehicle and is resampled into the ego frame of every new capture group, as in temporal fusion of birds-eye-view features [21], the IoU falls by 3.86, most on unchanged space, by 4.38, and by 3.02 on unseen space, against 0.42 on changed space. Resampling the state at every capture group blurs what it has seen, and the extra resampling lowers the speed to 21.29 FPS. Figure 6. Effect of the reset period of the state at evaluation on Occ3D-nuScenes, for the model trained with =8. Current frame: estimate of the current frame; forecasts averaged over 13 and 18 s. Shaded band: the reset period used in training. The image features must be learned: with the image encoder frozen, the mIoU falls by 4.07 and the IoU on unchanged space by 2.78. The Evolver is what completes unseen space: without it, the state is read unchanged at each target pose, and the IoU on unseen space falls by 12.22, against 3.66 and 2.43 on unchanged and changed space. Removing the depth conditioning or attention of the Writer, or the shared context of the Evolver, also lowers the accuracy of both the current frame and the forecasts, as the component ablations in Sec. show. Streaming. Updating the state as stream doubles the speed at nearly the same accuracy. Rebuilding the state for every query from the last eight capture groups reaches 29.26 mIoU and 67.97 IoU, against 28.72 and 67.82, but even with image features cached, every query then writes eight capture groups, and the speed nearly halves to 12.02 FPS. Copied forward, this input reaches only 46.31 IoU on unchanged space, and our state written from it reaches 72.06 there. The state combines the predictions of successive frames at fixed places in the scene, so it holds more of the seen scene than any single prediction. Running the perception network first, however, slows the model to 3.61 FPS, while state learned end to end from images needs no separate perception network. Memory span. forecast needs only the last few seconds of observation. We vary the reset period of the state at evaluation, for the model trained with =8  (Fig. 6)  . The estimate of the current frame improves with every added capture group, from 61.14 IoU at =1 to 68.99 at =16, as the evidence of successive frames accumulates in the state. Forecasts at 13 level off at =8 and change by at most 0.15 IoU beyond it, and the 18 average varies by at most 0.49. Resetting the state every eight capture groups thus costs no forecasting accuracy. 4.5. Qualitative Results Fig. 7 shows forecasts of our model and the ground truth in two scenes, at the current frame and 1, 2, and 3 ahead. In scene (a), the vehicle drives along construction zone with moving traffic and pedestrians; the buildings, vegetation, and sidewalks along the road stay in place in our forecasts up to 3 s, as in the ground truth, and the pedestrians on the right of the road remain in them. In scene (b), the vehicle crosses an intersection, and our forecast continues the road into space that no input frame observed. Comparisons with SparseWorld-TC on these and more scenes, forecasts from one state along two trajectories, and errors by distance and by dynamic and static classes are in Secs. to F. 5. Conclusion Sorting the future scene into unchanged, changed, and unseen space shows that camera-based occupancy forecasting is limited first by how well models hold on to what they have already seen. PersistWorld holds it in 3D world state anchored in the scene and updated as stream, and an evolver predicts the state at any queried time along the ego trajectory. On Occ3D-nuScenes, this raises the IoU of the best camera-based world model by 19 points at 13 and keeps the lead up to 8 s, at more than twice its speed.

sections.title: Appendix
sections.content: This appendix extends the experiments of Sec. 4. Sec. gives implementation details, Sec. writes the state from occupancy instead of images, Sec. removes components of the model one at time, Sec. breaks the forecasts down by class, distance, horizon, state depth, and ego motion, Sec. forecasts along trajectories other than the ground truth, and Sec. discusses more qualitative results. All results use the protocol of Sec. 4.1 unless stated otherwise. A. Implementation details Images are resized to 256704 and, during training, augmented as in SparseWorld-TC [9] by random scaling, cropping, flipping, and photometric distortion. The last four blocks of DINOv3 are fine-tuned at one third of the base learning rate. The state has 384 channels; the Evolver has three residual blocks and three context blocks, and the Writer two attention layers. We train for 20 epochs with AdamW at learning rate of 3104, decayed to one third over the last four epochs, with gradients clipped at norm of 5, on six A800 GPUs in about 15 hours. B. Forecasting from occupancy Our model can be written from occupancy instead of images. For each new occupancy grid, the Writer reads the labels of the eight voxels covered by each sub-cell, embeds their class histogram, and applies gated update to the state; the Evolver and Reader are unchanged. We train two such variants with the schedule of the main model. Both use the same streaming protocol as the camera model: each new grid is written once into the state, which is reset every eight keyframes and at scene changes, so forecast uses one to eight keyframes since the last reset. PersistWorld-STC is written from the occupancy predicted by STCOcc [25], the perception network of the two-stage methods, and is scored inside the camera mask. PersistWorld-GT is written from the ground-truth occupancy and is scored on the full volume, as the Occ GT methods in Tab. 1. Its 13 evaluation uses 4519 anchors with at least 2 of history and 3 of future available in the scene; this selects the scored anchors and does not change the state reset schedule. Each block of Tab. 4 also moves the input of the current frame to the target frame with the ego poses, which forecasts as if nothing changed. Occupancy-input forecasting. Using STCOcc predictions as the input source, PersistWorld-STC reaches 28.39 mIoU and 67.73 IoU on average, against 24.70 and 42.47 for GASTSTC, the strongest two-stage method. From the ground truth, PersistWorld-GT reaches 42.42 mIoU and 60.77 IoU, against 45.33 and 55.09 for GAST: it is the most accurate in geometry and third in semantics. PersistWorld-STC also exceeds the camera end-to-end baselines in Tab. 1, while reaching similar accuracy to our camera model. Compared with copying only the current occupancy forward, the full model gains 30.11 IoU with STCOcc input and 7.93 with ground-truth input. Same forecaster, different inputs. The three versions of our model share the Evolver and Reader and differ only in what is written into the state. Writing from images reaches 28.72 mIoU and 67.82 IoU in Tab. 1, against 28.39 and 67.73 when writing STCOcc predictions with the same streaming update and reset schedule. The state that the Writer learns from images, trained end to end with the forecast, is thus as useful to the forecast as the output of dedicated perception network trained on the same images. Up to 8 s. Tab. 5 queries PersistWorld-GT at every horizon from 1 to 8 in the long-horizon setting of COME, which GAST also follows. PersistWorld-GT reaches 34.43 mIoU and 50.82 IoU on average over 18 s, against 24.12 and 39.06 for GAST, and the warped current ground truth reaches 31.24 and 43.08. C. Component ablations Tab. 6 removes one component of the model at time; each variant is trained with the schedule of the main model. Without depth conditioning, the ray-depth head is still trained with the ray term, but neither its section embedding nor its log-probability enters the Writer. Mean writing averages the samples of each sub-cell instead of attending to them, so neither the learned query nor the depth bias weights the evidence. Without the shared context, the Evolver advances the state from the window around the ego alone. Every component improves both the estimate of the current frame and the forecasts. The ray-depth sections matter most for the current frame, by 1.66 mIoU and 1.30 IoU, as they decide at which depth along ray the evidence of an image is written. D. Detailed results Per class. Tab. 7 lists the IoU of every class. Our model gains most on terrain, manmade, drivable surface, sidewalk, and pedestrian, by 12.20 to 5.90 IoU, and SparseWorldTC remains ahead on construction vehicle and barrier, by 3.97 and 1.40 IoU. The large static classes, drivable surface, sidewalk, terrain, manmade, and vegetation, make up most of the occupied space, and our model is ahead on all five of them. 11 Table 4. The state is reset after every eight capture groups, so keyframe is answered with state that holds between one and eight of them. Tab. 10 groups the keyframes by this number. The estimate of the current frame improves quickly after reset, from 61.20 IoU with one capture group to 67.70 with two and 70.29 with eight. From three groups on, the forecast stays within 1 IoU of the 68.50 it reaches with eight. The state thus recovers within about 1.5 after reset, three capture groups at 0.5 spacing, which is why short memory span costs little. Every 0.5 s. Because the Evolver takes the ego trajectory up to the target time as input, the model can be queried at any time, including times it is never trained on. Below 3 s, the losses supervise only 1, 2, and 3 s; Tab. 9 also queries 0.5, 1.5, and 2.5 s. Our accuracy decreases steadily across all horizons, and every half-second horizon lies between its whole-second neighbors: from 1.5 to 7.5 s, it deviates from their linear interpolation by at most 0.22 mIoU and 0.79 IoU. For SparseWorld-TC, the IoU at 1.5 and 2.5 falls below both whole-second neighbors, 1.59 IoU under the interpolation at 2.5 s. Our forecast thus varies continuously with the queried time. Ego motion. How much of the target scene must be forecast depends on how the ego vehicle moves, and Tab. 11 groups the keyframes accordingly. In IoU, both methods are most accurate when the ego vehicle drives straight, less accurate when it stops, and least accurate in turns, where the target view swings into space that the input frames saw at grazing angles or not at all. Our model reaches 68.88, 64.07, and 63.24 IoU in these three cases, and our margin over SparseWorld-TC is 19.07, 19.50, and 19.80 IoU. The margin is thus nearly the same for every kind of ego motion. Trajectory conditioning Following the protocol of prior work [9, 11, 26, 35], Tab. 1 gives every method the ground-truth future ego poses. deployed system would instead forecast along planned trajectory, so we query both models with trajectories that are not the ground truth. Constant velocity extrapolates the last observed ego motion; the planned trajectories are the BEV-Planner [23] predictions released by COME [35], from the planner that SparseWorld-TC also uses.
